To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the transmission patterns of the lungs of normal subjects are different from those of subjects with emphysema, and that the transmission patterns are also different for different lung regions in the same subject.
sound transmission in human lung is frequency dependent, and that the frequency dependence is consistent with the predictions of an acoustical lung model.

the transmission of sound in human lungs is highly directional, that the directionality is strongly dependent on lung volume and that the directionality of sound transmission is similar for different subject groups.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the measurement of sound transmission through human and animal lungs and thoracic cavities.

the development and validation of a noninvasive technique to measure the sound transmission characteristics of the lung and thoracic structures and to use this technique as a tool in the investigation of the structure of the lung parenchymal and airway systems.
the use of sound transmission in the human lung as a diagnostic tool for lung disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transmission patterns of sound in the human lungs are consistent with a waveguide model of the lung parenchymal tissues and that the waveguide model can be applied to predict transmission patterns in the human lung for frequencies up to 20 kHz.

sound transmission through human lung parenchymal structures is highly frequency dependent, with the frequency dependence varying from subject to subject, and the transmission pattern in the frequency range 5–20 kHz can be used to differentiate between different subject groups, but the acoustic transmission pattern is not sufficiently sensitive to differentiate between different lung diseases.
the lung is a complex acoustic structure, which can be characterized in terms of a series of acoustical parameters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have shown that acoustic lung transmission measurements are feasible, that the transmission patterns can be measured with high repeatability, and that the measurements can be used to identify and quantify differences in lung structure between subject groups.
the transmission of sound through the lung parenchymal tissue appears to be frequency dependent, and that the transmission is greater for the larger airways than for the smaller airways.
the transmission patterns measured for all subject groups are similar, and that the measured transmission patterns are in general agreement with those predicted by the lung model.
The main takeaway from our work is that

sound transmission in the lungs is a promising method to reveal information about the structure and mechanics of the lungs, and that the instrumentation and methods developed here are a significant step toward making that information available to the medical community.
the transmission of sound through the human thorax is dominated by the lung parenchymal transmission, with a small contribution from the transmission through the rib cage.
the acoustic lung transmission pattern is a unique and sensitive measure of lung structure.
